_note: Short plain-language description of WHAT each entry's subject is (dataset, paper or code), shown before the finding. Keyed by register row number, or by id for custom entries.
2: RTE+RRTMGP is the radiative-transfer code that computes how sunlight and infrared radiation are absorbed and emitted by gases, clouds and aerosols. It is the radiation scheme in several major climate models, including CESM3, E3SM and ICON.
3: The COARE algorithm calculates the exchange of heat, moisture and momentum between the ocean surface and the atmosphere (air–sea fluxes). Versions of it are used in the coupling code of climate models such as CESM (CMEPS), E3SM and NorESM.
4: climate_indices is a Python package that computes drought indices such as the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), which expresses rainfall over a period as a number of standard deviations from normal.
5: SPEI is the R package, written by the index's developers, that computes the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and the Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), two of the most widely used drought indices.
6: xclim is a Python library from Ouranos (Montreal) for computing climate indices from model and observational data. Its SPI function converts rainfall totals into a standardized drought index.
7: martinvonk/SPEI is a Python package for computing standardized drought indices (SPI, SPEI) from rainfall and evaporation series.
8: climdex.pcic is the R package from the Pacific Climate Impacts Consortium that computes the 27 ETCCDI climate-extremes indices (hot days, warm spells, heavy rain and so on). Its output feeds the HadEX3 global extremes dataset and CMIP6 index sets.
9: CDO (Climate Data Operators) is a widely used command-line toolkit for processing climate model and gridded data. Its etccdi operators compute the standard ETCCDI climate-extremes indices.
10: ClimPACT is the World Meteorological Organization's software for computing climate indices (extremes, heatwaves, drought) from station data, used by national weather services.
11: pyMannKendall is a Python package for the Mann–Kendall trend test and its variants, which test whether a time series has a monotonic trend, including versions that correct for autocorrelation.
12: modifiedmk is an R package of Mann–Kendall trend tests modified for serially correlated data. Its mmky() function implements the Yue–Wang variance correction.
13: The Hamed–Rao test is a version of the Mann–Kendall trend test that inflates the test's variance to allow for autocorrelation. It is implemented in pyMannKendall and modifiedmk.
14: xsdba (formerly xclim.sdba) is Ouranos's Python library for statistical bias adjustment of climate model output. Quantile Delta Mapping (QDM) corrects a model's distribution against observations while preserving its projected changes.
15: xclim's potential evapotranspiration (PET) functions estimate how much water the atmosphere could take up; the Thornthwaite method uses temperature only. Its heat index combines temperature and humidity into an apparent temperature.
16: The PCMDI Metrics Package (PMP), from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, is the standard software for benchmarking CMIP climate models against observations.
17: climpred is a Python package for verifying initialized decadal and seasonal climate predictions, including comparing them with uninitialized (free-running) model simulations.
18: Skyborn is a Python package for optimal fingerprinting, the regression method used to detect and attribute climate change to particular causes (greenhouse gases, aerosols, natural factors).
19: tcpyPI is the Python implementation of the potential-intensity algorithm (Bister and Emanuel), which estimates the maximum intensity a hurricane could reach given ocean and atmospheric conditions.
21: rwwa is World Weather Attribution's R code for extreme-event attribution: it fits extreme-value distributions that shift with global warming and estimates how much climate change altered an event's likelihood.
22: MMM-physics is NCAR's shared library of physics schemes for the WRF and MPAS weather models. The KIM TOFD option represents turbulent orographic form drag (the drag of small-scale terrain on the wind).
23: MetPy is a widely used Python library for meteorological calculations. Its vorticity and divergence functions compute rotation and spreading of the wind from gridded data.
24: wrf-python is NCAR's Python library for post-processing WRF model output. Updraft helicity is a diagnostic used to identify rotating thunderstorms (supercells).
25: GeoCAT-comp is NCAR's Python library of geoscience computations (the successor to NCL functions). Its seasonal-average routines compute DJF, MAM, JJA and SON means.
26: GeoCAT-comp's gradient() function computes spatial derivatives of gridded fields, used for example in moisture-convergence calculations.
27: xCDAT (Xarray Climate Data Analysis Tools) is a Python library, developed with DOE support, for common climate-data operations such as temporal and seasonal averaging.
28: xESMF is a Python package for regridding (interpolating) climate data between grids. Conservative regridding is meant to preserve totals such as rainfall or energy.
29: earthkit-meteo is ECMWF's Python library of meteorological calculations, including humidity and wet-bulb temperature functions.
31: CLIMADA is ETH Zurich's open-source platform for climate risk assessment. Its tropical-cyclone module models the wind field around a storm track (here the Emanuel–Rotunno 2011 profile).
33: hydroeval is a Python package of goodness-of-fit scores for hydrological models. The non-parametric Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE_NP) compares simulated and observed river flows using ranks.
36: eofs and xeofs are Python packages for Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) analysis, which finds the dominant spatial patterns of variability in climate data.
39: Three widely used reference products: the Global Warming Index (human-induced warming to date), the radiative-forcing series of the Indicators of Global Climate Change (IGCC), and Mark Zelinka's tables of climate sensitivity and feedbacks for CMIP models.
40: A group of climate and statistics packages and workflows we checked and found to be correct: forecast scoring (properscoring, xskillscore), kriging (PyKrige), thermal-comfort indices (thermofeel), model evaluation (ESMValCore), multivariate bias correction (MBC), PET in R SPEI, fire-weather indices (GEFF, xclim) and a heat–mortality workflow (dlnm).
42: The Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) is the network of about 900 automated weather stations at US airports. Its wind sensors were changed from cup anemometers to sonic sensors in 2005–09; ASOS wind data feed global wind-trend studies through HadISD and ISD.
43: NOAA's Hourly Precipitation Data (HPD) is the US archive of hourly rain-gauge totals from about 2,000 stations, used to study short-duration extreme rainfall and design storms (for example NOAA Atlas 14/15).
44: ICOADS (International Comprehensive Ocean-Atmosphere Data Set) is the main archive of ship, buoy and other marine surface observations since the 1600s. It underlies sea-surface-temperature datasets such as HadSST4 and ERSST.
45: IBTrACS (International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship) is NOAA's global archive of tropical-cyclone tracks and intensities, combining the records of the world's forecast agencies.
46: The ASOS humidity sensor (DTS1) replaced the earlier chilled-mirror dew-point sensors at US airport weather stations in 2002–06.
47: NOAA's Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature (OISST) v2.1 is a daily, 0.25° global map of sea-surface temperature blending satellite, ship and buoy data. It is the standard dataset for marine-heatwave studies.
49: Boers (2021, Nature Climate Change) reported early-warning signals that the Atlantic overturning circulation (AMOC) is losing stability; Boulton et al. (2022, Nature Climate Change) reported the same for the Amazon rainforest. Both use rising variance and autocorrelation tested against surrogate data.
52: Kossin et al. (2020, PNAS) reported that the global share of hurricanes reaching major intensity (Category 3+) rose over 1979–2017. The result is cited in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report.
53: Ali et al. (2026, npj Climate and Atmospheric Science) estimated how hurricane rainfall increases with sea-surface temperature, reporting about 21% more rain per degree of warming.
67: Jin and Pu (2026, npj Climate and Atmospheric Science) tested whether the rate of global warming has accelerated, using change-point searches on global temperature records.
68: Zeng et al. (2019, Nature Climate Change) reported that the long decline in global land wind speeds ('stilling') reversed after about 2010; Monerie et al. (2026, Climate Dynamics) studied the same wind trends. Both rely on station wind records, including US airport (ASOS) data.
81: Six widely cited studies we tested independently and found to hold: Earth's energy imbalance doubling (Mauritsen 2025), sea-level acceleration (Nerem 2018), coastal extremes (Dangendorf 2026), drought (Xu 2026), hourly rainfall extremes (Guerreiro 2018) and the IGCC 2025 marine-heatwave indicator.
82: lmoments3 is the Python library (maintained by Ouranos) that fits extreme-value distributions by L-moments; it is the engine behind xclim's distribution fits. standard_precip is a Python package for computing the Standardized Precipitation Index.
83: Hugonnet et al. (2021, Nature) mapped thinning of nearly all of the world's ~220,000 glaciers from satellite elevation data and reported that glacier mass loss accelerated over 2000–2019.
84: MERRA-2 is NASA's global atmospheric reanalysis. Its corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), which drives the land surface, is adjusted toward NOAA's CPC Unified daily gauge analysis over land.
pyextremes-gaps: pyextremes is a Python library for extreme-value analysis, used to estimate return levels (for example the 100-year flood or rainfall) from block maxima or peaks over a threshold.
